On 29 December 1911 the eighth Jebtsundamba Khutuktu, head of Buddhism in Mongolia, was enthroned in Urga as Bogd Khan, the holy ruler of an independent Mongolia. Mongol princes had declared independence weeks after the Xinhai Revolution broke the Qing dynasty, saying their loyalty had been to the Manchu emperor, not to China.

The Bogd Khan, born in Tibet in 1869, was the third highest figure in Tibetan Buddhism after the Dalai Lama and the Panchen Lama. His state was a Buddhist theocracy, and it took the Soyombo symbol as its emblem. Russia backed it, but only as an autonomous part of China, under the Kyakhta treaty of 1915. China ended that autonomy in 1919, and in 1921 the White Russian baron Ungern-Sternberg seized Urga and restored the Bogd Khan.

Later in 1921 Mongolian revolutionaries under Sükhbaatar, with the Red Army, took over and kept the Bogd Khan as a figurehead. When he died in 1924, the communists declared the Mongolian People's Republic and forbade the search for his next rebirth. Mongolia still dates its independence to 1911.
